title: requirements-to-architecture-translator
body: Type a plain-language business ask, get back a structured technical spec - systems touched, triggers, field mappings, and edge cases - in a hosted internal tool.

solve: Turns a business sentence into a first-draft architecture spec in seconds, so solution sessions start from a shared artifact instead of a blank page.
steps: Built on Claude with a saved, version-controlled internal prompt template that enforces the output structure - systems, trigger, data flow, field map, edge cases.
Wired in the Figma connector so the generated spec drops straight onto a shared design canvas the customer and engineers annotate together in the session.
Wrapped it in a lightweight web interface (input box, example chips, rendered spec sheet) so a non-technical stakeholder can drive it.
Hosted the interface on Vercel for a shareable internal URL - no local setup, always current.

title: config-review-ai-agent
body: An AI agent that reviews a customer's configuration and returns prioritized gaps, risks, and recommended fixes - an architecture review that runs itself.
pain: Six months after go-live, most implementations quietly drift - integrations nobody owns, manual steps meant to be automated. Spotting it takes a senior architect manually combing the config, so it rarely happens until something breaks.
solve: An agent inspects the live config, reasons about it against best practice, and returns a ranked list of gaps with fixes - so every account gets an expert review, not just the squeaky wheels.
steps: In Python, pulled an account's live configuration via the Productboard REST API as structured input for the agent.
Gave a Claude API agent a tool to read config plus a rubric of best-practice checks, each weighted by severity.
The agent reasons over the config, identifies gaps, and returns structured findings - issue, severity, and the specific recommended fix.
Findings render as a ranked scorecard that becomes the agenda for the customer's architecture review.
why: Built at Productboard to make account reviews objective and scalable. Instead of a static checklist, the agent reasons about each unique config - the same review an SA would run, on every account.

title: ai-workflow-orchestration-pipeline
body: Watch one real piece of customer feedback get cleaned, tagged, and routed automatically - the exact five-step pattern behind any "AI over messy customer data" workflow.
pain: A support ticket, an NPS comment, and a sales call note all describe the same problem in three different formats. Nobody has time to read all of it, tag it consistently, and get it to the right team - so patterns get missed.
solve: One message runs through five stages - clean it up, tag it, roll it into a theme, send it to the right team - fully automatically, in seconds instead of sitting in a queue for a week.
steps: Abstracted the workflow into five swappable stages - ingest, normalize, classify, summarize, deliver - so each could be reconfigured per customer.
In VS Code, wrote Python orchestration where the normalize and classify steps take config, not hardcoded rules.
Used LangChain for the conditional multi-step logic and standardized the LLM API calls so any stage's model or prompt could swap without touching the rest.
Documented it as an internal reference pattern so any engagement could start from the architecture instead of a blank file.
why: Built at Productboard as AI Technical Lead - the design abstraction that let one architecture serve many customers. The delivered version for a specific client lives in the Clients section.

title: integration-triage-diagnostic
body: Scenario: a customer's nightly Salesforce sync has failed three times this week with no obvious pattern. Walk the same questions a senior engineer would ask to reach the actual root cause.
pain: When a customer integration breaks, the fix often depends on which engineer picks up the ticket - the fastest diagnostic path lives in a couple of senior people's heads, so resolution time is inconsistent and senior staff get pulled into repeat triage.
solve: Encodes the expert debugging path into a guided flow, so first-touch resolution stops depending on who's available and senior engineers stop re-solving the same failures.
steps: Catalogued the recurring integration failures across the enterprise API accounts into a set of symptom categories.
For each symptom, mapped the branching questions a senior engineer actually asks to isolate the cause.
Encoded that logic as a decision tree in JavaScript, where each leaf resolves to a specific root cause and the exact fix.
Recorded the path taken on each run so resolutions were self-documenting for the next person.
why: Built from the escalation patterns I saw supporting Perigon's enterprise API accounts. A guided runbook like this cuts time-to-resolution and scales a support team's expertise across every integration a customer runs.

title: customer-health-risk-dashboard
body: One named account, real-looking usage signals, a computed risk score - then Claude writes the actual talking points a CSM would bring into the renewal conversation.
pain: By the time a renewal conversation reveals a customer is at risk, it's often too late. The warning signs were in the usage data months earlier, unread - and even when someone notices, turning a risk score into a concrete talking point takes time nobody has.
solve: Scores account health from real adoption signals, then generates the specific recommendation a CSM can act on today - not just a number, an actual next step.

Pulled usage data through the platform's analytics/SQL layer and mapped each score band to a recommended intervention.
Surfaced it as a dashboard the CS and product teams reviewed to prioritize outreach.
why: Built as Product Operations Manager at Sentieo (acquired by AlphaSense) to get ahead of churn. Directly the "proactively identify risks and opportunities within accounts" work a post-sales SA owns.

title: tool-consolidation-roi-model
body: Modeled from a real pattern at Productboard: a customer running four overlapping feedback and roadmap tools nobody had ever added up the true cost of.
pain: An enterprise customer was running a standalone feedback inbox, a separate roadmap tool, a survey tool, and a support-ticket tagger - four licenses, four integrations to maintain, and nobody had ever put a number on what the overlap actually cost.
solve: Puts a real dollar figure on consolidating onto one platform - current spend vs. platform spend, plus the integrations retired - so the SA and Account Manager walk in with a business case, not a pitch.
steps: In Python, modeled this customer's current-state monthly spend and integration count across their four overlapping tools.
Encoded the consolidation logic - which overlapping tools Productboard's platform absorbs, and the integration points that retire with them.
Output projected platform cost, monthly savings, and the number of integrations eliminated.
Walked the Account Manager through it live before the renewal call - the model became the leave-behind.
why: Built at Productboard after seeing this exact overlap on a real enterprise account. The "point solutions to a single platform" case a post-sales SA makes to grow an account, backed by numbers instead of enthusiasm.

title: analytics-warehouse-pipeline
body: At Sentieo, the product team could see feature clicks but not which research usage patterns actually predicted renewal - because that data lived in three different systems.
pain: Product usage lived in the app database, account tier lived in the billing system, and renewal outcomes lived in Salesforce. Answering "does research-heavy usage predict renewal" meant three exports and a afternoon in a spreadsheet, every single time someone asked.
solve: A clean analytical schema, fed automatically from all three operational systems, lets product and CS self-serve that question - and any question like it - in a single query.
steps: Designed a dimensional schema (fact + dimension tables) joining product usage, account tier, and renewal outcomes - the three metrics the business actually needed together.
Built an ETL job in Python to extract from all three operational systems incrementally and transform them into that schema.
Loaded into a Snowflake-style warehouse and wrote the SQL views the analytics layer sat on.
Exposed it so product and CS teams could self-serve usage-vs-renewal questions without a data engineer in the loop.
why: Built at Sentieo (acquired by AlphaSense) to answer the one question leadership kept asking that nobody could answer quickly. The exact data-flow work behind advising a customer on getting their data into Snowflake or Databricks.

title: geolocation-radius-validation
body: A news API sold "articles near this location". If the radius math is subtly wrong, customers get irrelevant results, never file a bug, and quietly stop trusting the feature.
pain: A radius filter that's subtly wrong doesn't throw an error - it just returns results that are almost right. Customers don't report "almost right," they just quietly pull full datasets and filter client-side instead, which spikes load and erodes trust in the API.
solve: Independently proves the radius math is correct before it ships, so 150+ enterprise clients could trust the filter enough to actually use it - directly cutting support tickets 24.7%.
steps: In VS Code, wrote a Python test script implementing the Haversine formula independently of the production code, as a ground-truth check.
Called the live API with the new radius parameter, then asserted every returned article actually fell within the declared radius using the independent calculation.
Built a Postman collection covering edge cases (boundary of radius, zero radius, antimeridian) for repeatable regression testing.
Wrote the client-facing API docs and ran release communication to the full enterprise client base.
why: Built at Perigon before shipping a geolocation filter to 150+ enterprise accounts. This is the validation discipline that makes a customer trust a feature enough to actually adopt it - not just ship it.

title: legacy-data-migration-automation
body: Automated a manual, multi-week enterprise data migration into a same-day process with built-in validation and human-review flagging.
pain: Every enterprise onboarding started with years of legacy feedback data in inconsistent formats - some CSV exports, some Salesforce dumps. Migrating it by hand took weeks and still shipped errors into the new system.
solve: Collapses a multi-week manual migration into a same-day, repeatable process where bad records are caught and flagged, not discovered by the customer after go-live.
steps: In VS Code, wrote a Python pipeline using pandas to ingest mixed CSV and Salesforce-export sources into one dataframe.
Normalized fields (names, dates, emails), then validated each row against the target JSON schema for the Productboard REST API.
Clean rows were batch-imported via the API; ambiguous rows were written to a review queue with the specific reason flagged.
Logged every insert and rejection so the customer had a full audit of what moved and what needed a human.
why: Built at Productboard to onboard enterprise customers faster without shipping data errors into their new environment.
proto: ▸ try it - run the cleaner on messy rows

title: salesforce-productboard-two-way-sync
body: A bi-directional integration connecting a client's Salesforce instance to Productboard - customer requests flowed in, roadmap decisions flowed back out, automatically.
pain: The client's sales team logged feature requests in Salesforce Opportunities, but product lived in Productboard. Someone re-typed every request by hand, and once product made a call, sales had no way of knowing without asking.
solve: One integration keeps both systems in sync - requests land in Productboard automatically, and roadmap status flows back onto the Salesforce record, so both teams work off the same truth.
steps: In VS Code, stood up a Python webhook listener to receive Salesforce Opportunity events in real time.
On a flagged Opportunity, mapped the record's fields to a structured feature note and created it in Productboard via the Productboard REST API.
Built the reverse path: a sync job read roadmap status and priority changes and wrote them back onto the originating Salesforce record through the Salesforce API.
Added retry with exponential backoff and an error queue so a failed call never silently dropped a record - both teams could trust the data.
why: Built for a Productboard enterprise client whose sales and product teams were maintaining the same list twice. The kind of CRM-to-system-of-record bridge post-sales customers need across their whole stack.

title: colleague-ai-productivity-agent

solve: A lightweight shared agent with a small set of grounded actions, wired to the same data sources already in use, with versioned prompt templates so answer quality stayed consistent across the team.

Wired each template to the actual data source it needed - Productboard API for feature status, CRM export for account activity.

Shared it as one internal tool with version-controlled prompts, instead of everyone maintaining their own ChatGPT thread.

solve: A scheduled job pulls the metrics leadership already tracks weekly and drafts the narrative summary automatically - flagging anything that moved notably so the exec knows what needs a story, and edits from there.

solve: Paste meeting notes, get back owned action items automatically, with a nudge at the due date - nothing said out loud gets lost.

Run them through an LLM prompt tuned specifically to identify action-bearing sentences vs. general discussion.

A single dashboard view replaces checking each vendor's portal manually.

title: visa-appointment-checker-bot
body: A Telegram bot that monitors Schengen visa appointment slots across consulates and pushes real-time availability alerts.
pain: Visa appointment slots open and disappear within minutes across multiple consulate sites - checking manually multiple times a day is impractical and slots are consistently missed.
solve: The bot polls every consulate on a schedule and pushes an alert the instant a slot opens, so you never have to babysit a webpage.
where: Personal project · solved my own visa logistics
steps: In VS Code, wrote a Python script that polls each consulate's appointment API/page on a cron schedule.
Parsed each response for open slots and diffed against the last known state to detect new availability.
On a new slot, called the Telegram Bot API to push an instant alert to my phone.
Stored credentials in environment variables, never hardcoded, and ran it unattended on a schedule.
why: Built to solve a real, personal logistics problem during my own visa process - small in scope, but it runs unattended and does its job every day.
